## Proof

**Answer: Yes.** Every $f \in \mathcal{L}^p(A)$ can be extended to a function $g \in \mathcal{L}^p(\overline{A})$.

**Setup.** Since $A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})$, its closure $\overline{A}$ is closed, hence also Borel, so both $A$ and $\overline{A}$ are Lebesgue measurable. We have the disjoint decomposition
$$\overline{A} = A \;\sqcup\; N, \qquad N := \overline{A}\setminus A,$$
and by hypothesis $N$ is a Lebesgue null set. We equip $A$ and $\overline{A}$ with Lebesgue measure (restricted to each), and since $N \subseteq \overline{A}$ is Lebesgue null, it remains null under the restriction to $\overline{A}$.

**Construction.** Given $f \in \mathcal{L}^p(A)$, define $g : \overline{A} \to \mathbb{R}$ by
$$
g(x) = \begin{cases} f(x), & x \in A, \\ 0, & x \in N. \end{cases}
$$

**Measurability.** The set $A$ is Borel (hence Lebesgue measurable in $\overline{A}$), and $N = \overline{A}\setminus A$ is Lebesgue measurable (it is null). Since $f$ is measurable on $A$ and the constant $0$ is measurable on $N$, the piecewise definition yields a measurable function on $\overline{A}$.

**Integrability.** Using $\overline{A} = A \sqcup N$ and $|g|^p = |f|^p \cdot \mathbf{1}_A + 0 \cdot \mathbf{1}_N$,
$$
\int_{\overline{A}} |g|^p \,d\lambda \;=\; \int_A |f|^p\,d\lambda \;+\; \int_N 0\,d\lambda \;=\; \int_A |f|^p\,d\lambda \;<\; \infty.
$$
Hence $g \in \mathcal{L}^p(\overline{A})$, and moreover $\|g\|_{\mathcal{L}^p(\overline{A})} = \|f\|_{\mathcal{L}^p(A)}$ (the extension is isometric).

**Well-definedness on equivalence classes.** If $\mathcal{L}^p$ is interpreted as a space of equivalence classes modulo null sets, the construction is still well-defined: modifying $f$ on a $\lambda$-null subset $Z \subseteq A$ modifies $g$ only on $Z \subseteq \overline{A}$, which is null in $\overline{A}$. Thus the class $[g]$ depends only on $[f]$, and the map $[f] \mapsto [g]$ is a linear isometric embedding $\mathcal{L}^p(A) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{L}^p(\overline{A})$.

**Why the null-set hypothesis is essential.** The argument hinges entirely on $N$ being null: it guarantees that whatever values we assign on $N$ contribute nothing to the $L^p$-norm, so the extension is automatic. If $N$ had positive measure, arbitrary extension would generally fail (one would need to define $g$ on a set of positive measure with no information from $f$, and there is no canonical way to keep $g \in L^p$). The hypothesis $N = \overline{A}\setminus A$ being null is precisely what makes $A$ and $\overline{A}$ indistinguishable from the measure-theoretic standpoint.

**Conclusion.** Under the assumption that $N = \overline{A}\setminus A$ is a Lebesgue null set, every $f \in \mathcal{L}^p(A)$ extends to $g \in \mathcal{L}^p(\overline{A})$ (e.g. by zero on $N$), with preservation of the $L^p$-norm.

### PROOF COMPLETE
